title: Claude Code's “Don't Ask Again” File Exposes Passwords and Keys in 1,122 Public Copies on GitHub
why: If you ever approved a shell command containing an inline password or token in Claude Code, that secret may already be on a public GitHub default branch, and deleting the file does not remove it from git history or forks.
notes: Apiiro scanned 104,185 public copies of .claude/settings.local.json across 103,617 repos; 1,122 copies (about 1.1%) held at least one secret, 1,379 secrets total. The firm did not test whether the keys still work, though one notified company confirmed its key was live.

Mechanism: picking 'Yes, and don't ask again' saves an allow rule. When the prompt offers the exact command rather than a pattern like npm test *, the whole command, including any inline password or token, is stored in plaintext. Reproduced on Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1.

Leak persistence: Claude Code adds the file only to the user's global git excludes on first write, never to the project .gitignore, so the protection does not travel and does nothing for already-committed files. A Claude co-authored commit changed the file in 539 of 1,105 traced repos. Every secret-bearing file was still on the default branch as of Monday, there a median 217+ days.

Secret breakdown: over a third open a database directly (379 DB passwords), plus 43 SSH logins for public servers, 42 GitHub/GitLab/npm tokens, and 23 AWS keys, spread across 63 organizations. Named standouts (per the researchers): a database vendor's admin-level cloud key and a medical-records DB owner password. Counting git history, forks, committed settings.json, and agent logs raises the total to 2,539 secrets across 1,994 repos.

Scanner blind spot: run without verification, gitleaks flagged 564 and TruffleHog 643 of the 1,122 files; neither caught 215. Misses are passwords typed after PGPASSWORD=, sshpass -p, or mysql -p, which look like ordinary words to key-format scanners.

Of 16 coding agents whose docs were compared, Claude Code is the only one confirmed to save full approved commands in a project file by default. A bug report filed 2025-08-11 and three related reports were all closed by an automated bot as 'not planned' with no reply from Anthropic, per the researchers.
summary: Security firm Apiiro reports that Claude Code's 'Yes, and don't ask again' option can save approved shell commands verbatim, including any inline password, token, or key, into the project file .claude/settings.local.json, and that these secrets have leaked to public GitHub. Of 104,185 public copies scanned, 1,122 held at least one secret, for 1,379 secrets total, including 379 database passwords, 43 SSH logins, 42 Git/npm tokens, and 23 AWS keys across 63 organizations; the researchers did not verify whether the keys still work, though one notified company confirmed a live key. Claude Code adds the file only to a single machine's global git excludes, never to the project .gitignore, so the protection does not travel, and a Claude co-authored commit added the file in 539 of 1,105 traced repos. Deleting the file does not fix the exposure because secrets remain in git history and forks; the recommended order is to rotate every credential first, then clean up. Common scanners miss many cases: run without verification, gitleaks and TruffleHog together failed to flag 215 of the 1,122 files, mostly passwords passed as command flags like PGPASSWORD=. The researchers say Claude Code is the only one of 16 compared agents confirmed to save full approved commands by default, and that four related bug reports since August 2025 were all closed by an automated bot with no Anthropic response.
novelty: quantified secret leakage via Claude Code's auto-approve settings file
audience: developers and security teams using AI coding agents

title: AI Proved the Quasi-Riemann Hypothesis. What Happens Now?
why: An AI system settled a weaker form of the 160-year-old Riemann hypothesis that number theorists say carries most of RH's consequences, and it did so by recombining existing tools rather than inventing new math, shifting the open question from "can models do real research math" to "can we verify and read what they produce."
notes: OpenAI announced the quasi-RH proof on October 6, 2026 as part of a large batch of results (the article cites both 377 and 722 papers in different passages). Two versions exist: a September 30 version proving all nontrivial zeros lie between 1/8 and 7/8 (199 pages, formally verified in Lean), and a later ~49-page version proving a weaker 1/12-to-11/12 bound (not yet formally verified).

Mathematicians are concentrating on the shorter 11/12 paper, which Radziwiłł calls the only one of the batch edited by a human; OpenAI declined to say who edited it, responding only that the paper 'is the result of work from everyone at OpenAI.'

Quasi-RH narrows the strip containing the zeta function's nontrivial zeros rather than pinning them to the 1/2 line; Radziwiłł says 'the vast majority of consequences of RH already follow from quasi-RH,' spanning number theory, geometry, and theoretical CS.

The proof introduces no new concepts: it synthesizes known ideas, including a 2021 formula by Dunn and Radziwiłł and metaplectic forms Dunn had studied for five years. It realizes Sarnak's decades-old strategy of treating zeta as one member of a function family, using a family Iwaniec narrowly missed in 2002.

Reviewers say the papers are 'horribly written' and would be rejected by any journal; Sarnak is repurposing a course to study it and won't call it 'a Theorem' until humans check every detail. Radziwiłł can now sketch the argument in half a page; private write-ups run 7-13 pages. Experts (Sawin) expect the technique cannot reach the full 1/2 bound, though Bloom notes they'd have said the same about quasi-RH weeks earlier.
summary: Quanta reports that on October 6, 2026, OpenAI announced a claimed proof of the quasi-Riemann hypothesis, a weaker form of the Riemann hypothesis that confines the zeta function's nontrivial zeros to a strip narrower than (0,1) rather than fixing them on the real-part-1/2 line. Two versions circulate: a 199-page September 30 proof of a 1/8-to-7/8 bound that was formally verified in Lean, and a shorter ~49-page proof of a weaker 1/12-to-11/12 bound that is not yet verified; mathematicians are focusing on the shorter one, reportedly the only paper in the batch to receive human editing. Number theorists including Radziwiłł, Dunn, Sarnak, and Lichtman largely judge the result correct and call its consequences staggering, since most implications of full RH follow from quasi-RH. The proof's claimed novelty is a synthesis of existing tools, notably metaplectic forms and a 2021 Dunn-Radziwiłł formula, realizing Sarnak's long-standing family-of-functions strategy using a family overlooked since Iwaniec's 2002 work. Reviewers criticize the papers as poorly written by journal standards, and Sarnak withholds the label Theorem pending full human verification. Experts doubt the method extends to the full RH, while cautioning that quasi-RH itself looked out of reach weeks earlier.
novelty: AI proves quasi-Riemann hypothesis via synthesis of known techniques, not new concepts
audience: mathematicians and AI-for-science researchers tracking AI's role in formal proof generation

title: The 'Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen' post is misleading
why: The headline "reads and writes weights to improve Qwen" result actually ran the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems and wrote Python, so treating it as evidence that a model can edit real LLMs by inspection alone misreads what was demonstrated.
notes: The abstract's claim that Astra works 'just by looking at the raw weights' holds only for experiments 1, 2, and 4, on tiny networks of 17K to 172K weights, with no tools and without running the network.

The headline Qwen3.5-0.8B result (MATH-500 7.9% to 48.1%, IFEval up 3x via editing 0.016% of weights) used Python code and ran the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems; every experiment involving a real language model used Python.
The from-scratch MinAtar networks beat PPO-500M only on Breakout (517 vs 25) and lose on Seaquest (53 vs 89) and Asterix (53 vs 55); their weights start at zero, so there is nothing to read.

Fixing a stuck Kinetix car policy (0% to 100%) changed 3.5% of weights in one try after being given one recorded failure episode; spotting a sycophantic Gemma 3 failed with Python alone but passed 3/3 once shown attention patterns across up to 16 texts.

Author's core objection: the post bundles two distinct techniques, direct raw-weight inspection and Python-assisted analysis with model execution, under one narrative; a single technique doing both would imply a deep 'gestalt' capability, which was not tested here.

Author concedes the Python-assisted Qwen work is real engineering that models from a year or two ago would have failed, likening the mixed methods to a stage magician performing the same trick multiple ways.
summary: A critique argues that the "Astra can read and write weights to improve Qwen" post conflates fundamentally different techniques under a misleading "just by looking at the raw weights" framing. Using a per-experiment table, the author shows that pure raw-weight reading (floats in context, no tools, no model execution) appears only in three experiments on 17K-172K-weight networks. The headline Qwen3.5-0.8B result, raising MATH-500 from 7.9% to 48.1% by editing 0.016% of weights, instead relied on writing Python and running the model on up to 50 batches of practice problems; every real-LLM experiment used Python. Other results are similarly qualified: the from-scratch MinAtar networks beat PPO-500M only on Breakout, and the Kinetix fix was given a recorded failure episode. The author grants this is genuine work mirroring what human ML engineers do and beyond year-old models, but objects that no single technique was shown to both author small networks from scratch and understand a large existing model, so the post overstates a unified deep capability.
novelty: debunks claim that single technique reads weights to improve models
audience: ML researchers and engineers evaluating interpretability/weight-editing claims

title: The Components of Agent Memory
why: If you build agents, this is Anthropic's working recipe for persistent memory: let the model judge what to save in-session, then run "dreaming" (offline passes over transcripts) to correct wrong notes and build wiki indexes, with measured gains like 13%→48% accuracy as dreaming scaled to 128 sessions.
notes: "Dreaming" is Anthropic's term for offline memory reorganization, borrowed from the Letta/UC Berkeley "sleep-time compute" idea: the agent reflects on logs during idle time to fix mistakes and build new representations. Agent memory is defined narrowly as knowledge saved as re-readable context between sessions, explicitly excluding weight updates, in-context learning, and compaction.

On CL-Bench 1.0 (continual learning via a persisted memory directory across fresh sessions), capability scaled with model: Sonnet 4.6 only generated untested theories, Opus 5 was first to "close the loop" (rules plus evidence plus trap warnings); Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5 matched Opus 5. Note the article names unreleased models: Opus 4.7, Opus 5, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5, Sonnet 5.5, and "Fable 5."

Pokémon Red salience test: Sonnet 3.7 wrote indiscriminately (413 files across 225 folders, 1 badge) and stalled recombing stale notes; Fable 5 wrote 9 files in 2 folders plus a global.md dashboard and earned 4 badges; Opus 5.5 beat the game. Lesson: don't store what's readable from screen state; store only strategy and tested rules.

Steering finding reversing conventional prompt advice: for stronger models, fixed rules like "record only failures" cut the memory boost (hurt Opus 5 and 4.7); freedom to judge salience won. Steering helped older models most: prompting Sonnet 4.6 to read memory and test theories nearly doubled its score, behavior Sonnet 5 does unprompted (reads memory 9/10 times vs under half for 4.6).

Wiki representation tested on Stainless corpus (~350k files, ~420M tokens, acquired May): across 128 dreaming sessions, grading on 25 questions rose from 13% to 48%. Search+wiki beat search alone (61% vs 53%) and saved ~20k tokens/question. Caveats: on a Harvey LAB brief task the wiki grew larger than the source docs (Borges map analogy) and added nothing; dreaming requires compute and injected top-layer notes burn tokens and can propagate a wrong note into every session.

Instruction-tuning the wiki build mattered: a shared contract-terms table where parallel agents overwrote each other yielded 72% of facts (41/57); giving each contract its own page with verbatim quotes, discovered via a reflect-and-rebuild loop, reached 100%.
summary: Anthropic lays out a taxonomy and set of internal evaluations for agent memory, defined as knowledge Claude saves as re-readable context between sessions (excluding weight updates, in-context learning, and compaction). The central mechanism is "dreaming," offline reflection over session transcripts (derived from the Letta/UC Berkeley "sleep-time compute" concept) used to correct wrong notes, promote notes up a hierarchy, and build wiki representations. Evaluations span CL-Bench 1.0 (where capability to "close the learning loop" improved from Sonnet 4.6 up to Opus 5 and beyond), Pokémon Red (where salience judgment separated profligate Sonnet 3.7 from concise Fable 5), the Stainless document corpus (~420M tokens, where scaling dreaming to 128 sessions raised QA accuracy from 13% to 48% and search+wiki beat search alone), and Harvey LAB legal-brief tasks. Reported lessons: tell Claude what memory is for but not how to use it; fixed salience rules can hurt stronger models; and dreaming's cost and failure modes (bloated wikis, propagated errors, token-heavy context injection) require tuned cadence. All numbers are Anthropic's own self-reported results; some evaluated models (Opus 4.7/5/5.5, Sonnet 5/5.5, Fable 5) are not publicly released, and methodology details are limited to what the post describes.
novelty: Anthropic's taxonomy of agent memory: dreaming, salience prediction, consolidation
audience: engineers building long-horizon AI agents with persistent memory

title: Faster Retrieval for Better, More Efficient RAG
why: If your RAG queries come from a stable, known distribution, training a small offline network per key database cuts retrieval latency up to ~8x at 99% recall while reusing your existing FAISS/IVF index.
notes: Core insight: the function mapping a query to its largest inner product over a key set is the support function from convex analysis; it is convex (approximable by input convex neural networks) and its gradient returns the best-matching key.

Two variants: SupportNet (loosely-constrained ICNN producing k cluster scores to replace centroid routing) and KeyNet (regresses the query directly to its best-matching key, kept consistent via a loss from Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions). KeyNet acts as a query rewriter in front of a standard IVF index.
Benchmark: Natural Questions, ~2.6M passages, 128 clusters; model sizes XS/S/M/L correspond to 1%/5%/10%/20% of database size. All self-reported Apple numbers.

SupportNet claims: small model hits 95% routing recall ~1.9x faster than centroid routing (1.74 ms vs 3.36 ms, overhead included); large model hits 97% at 1.74 ms. At a 5%-of-database budget, learned routers find the true partition ~90-93% of the time vs 87.5% for centroid.

KeyNet claims: 99% recall in ~8x less wall-clock time (0.23 ms vs 1.8 ms raw query); scanning 0.001% of the database retrieves the true key 89-97% of the time (up to 96.7% for L) vs 86% raw; 99% recall needs ~11x fewer keys scanned (0.009% vs 0.10%).

Caveats: method assumes a fixed key database and a known, stable query distribution; training requires precomputing ground-truth best matches via exhaustive search; authors report only 'reasonable' robustness to mild query distribution shift, and results shown are on Natural Questions via a FAISS IVF index.
summary: Apple researchers (ICML 2026 paper, "Amortizing Maximum Inner Product Search with Learned Support Functions") propose training small neural networks offline, per fixed key database, to accelerate maximum inner product search for queries drawn from a known distribution. The method exploits that the query-to-best-match function is the support function of the key set, a convex object whose gradient yields the best key. Two models are offered: SupportNet, an input convex network that outputs per-cluster scores to replace error-prone centroid routing in IVF indexes, and KeyNet, which rewrites a query into its predicted best-matching key and feeds it to a standard approximate index. On Natural Questions (~2.6M passages, 128 clusters), Apple reports SupportNet reaching 95% routing recall ~1.9x faster than centroid routing, and KeyNet reaching 99% recall with up to ~8x less latency and ~11x fewer keys scanned. The trade-off is a one-time amortization cost and a dependence on a stable, well-characterized query distribution; the authors recommend KeyNet when inference speed dominates and SupportNet when a calibrated score is needed. All performance figures are vendor self-reported on the datasets studied.
novelty: learned support functions amortize MIPS routing for known query distributions
audience: ML engineers building RAG/retrieval and recommendation infra at scale

title: Show HN: Klad, a paint app your coding agent can drive (source-available)
why: If you build games or illustration tooling, this gives an agent a brush that outputs editable strokes instead of pixels, so you fix one bad leaf by hand instead of re-rolling the whole image.
notes: No generative image model: the agent (Claude Code, Codex, anything that runs commands) decides what to paint and does it through the `klad` CLI. Every stroke and fill persists as data (path, pressure, brush, colour) you or the agent can recolour, bend, move, or delete hours later.

The CLI mirrors every editor action (stroke, set, fill, strokes --json, inbetween, export, undo) and applies batches of edits as JSON ops; a drawing is a folder of plain files, no account, so it versions in git. File format and CLI are documented and MIT-licensed, so other apps can read/write drawings.

Self-reported demo (drawings made with 'Claude Fable 5.2'): a 'sprout creature' is 4,344 strokes and fills, animated by sorting parts into five groups with 205 keys and no frame repainted; no methodology or comparison given.

Source-available, not open source (PolyForm Internal Use 1.0.0, copyright Indicode BV): free to build and use personally or inside a company under EUR 500k/year revenue; at or above that, each user needs a bought licence. Only docs/format.md, docs/cli.md, docs/skill/ and crates/client are MIT.

Full 2D paint and animation app: ~two dozen brushes plus editor, layers/masks/clipping, vector shapes with gradients and ~50 fonts, oil/smudge that blend on relocation, timeline with onion skins, bones with IK (preview, commands may change), exports to PNG, sprite sheets, or a Godot SpriteFrames scene.

Early first public release with no installers; you compile from source (Rust, just; ~10 min first build). Pen pressure and tilt are macOS-only; Linux starts with mouse (no tablet pressure) and Windows builds and passes tests but is undrawn. Missing: multi-select, align/distribute, snapping, grid, SVG import/export.
summary: Klad is a source-available 2D painting and animation app designed to be driven by a coding agent alongside a human, with no generative image model: the agent decides what to paint and executes strokes through the `klad` command line, while the human paints with a pen, and both see each other's strokes in about a second. Every mark is kept as editable data (path, pressure, brush, colour; shapes with points; fills with regions), so edits target individual strokes rather than re-rolling a generated image. The CLI mirrors all editor actions and takes batches of JSON ops; drawings are plain-file folders that version in git, and the file format, CLI, agent skills, and client crate are MIT even though the app itself is under PolyForm Internal Use (free below EUR 500k company revenue, paid licence per user above). The app includes layers, masks, oil/smudge brushes, vector tooling, bones with IK (preview), in-betweens, and export to PNG, sprite sheets, or Godot. A self-reported demo painted a creature as 4,344 strokes and animated it with 205 keys across five groups without repainting frames. Status is early: no installers, compile-from-source only, pen pressure is macOS-only, and Linux/Windows drawing is untested or mouse-only.
novelty: agent-drivable paint/animation app with no image model, stroke-level data
audience: devs building creative tooling or agent-driven game/art pipelines

title: A false smoke alarm almost drowned Jane Street's only NYC datacenter
why: The failure chain here is a default you probably share: a smoke alarm wired to kill the CRAC units turns a dust-triggered false alarm into a thermal runaway that pre-charges the sprinklers over your racks.
notes: Jane Street kept its only NYC datacenter inside 1 New York Plaza (33rd floor), next to the trading floor, for two stated reasons: IP theft fears and a last-resort physical kill switch, pull the power cords, a culture the author attributes partly to a partner with nuclear-submarine experience.

The sprinkler design was dry-pipe: pipes stay empty to avoid overhead leaks, a separate detector fills them with pressurized water on smoke, and each head sprays only when its own heat-sensitive plug melts (around 150 F in the telling).

The near-miss: smoke detection was also wired to shut off the CRAC cooling units to avoid feeding a fire; a contractor cutting in an adjacent prep room kicked up dust, tripped the alarm with no actual fire, and the room heated with pressurized pipes already primed overhead.

The author sprinted from a nearby apartment and manually yanked power from every rack; the temperature monitor peaked at 143.6 F before stopping. Markets were closed, so downtime was minimal and systems were back the next morning.

Detection was luck: Hong Kong staff noticed many servers reporting climbing temperatures at once; no single server alerted on being 'a little hot.' The fix was an OCaml monitor that polls every server's onboard temperature sensors each minute, averages them, and alerts on an elevated fleet-wide mean, deliberately trusting server sensors over less reliable CRAC or room-sensor telemetry.

First-person war story, self-reported and unverified; the post-incident decision was to keep the sprinklers, tighten procedures and surveillance, and keep the datacenter in the office until Hurricane Sandy, which the author leaves for a later piece. Disclosed as human-written with AI proofreading.
summary: A former Jane Street systems engineer recounts a near-disaster at the firm's only NYC datacenter, co-located with the trading floor inside 1 New York Plaza for IP-security and manual-kill-switch reasons. A contractor's cutting dust triggered a false smoke alarm; the alarm was wired to shut down the CRAC cooling units and to pressurize the dry-pipe sprinklers overhead, so with no fire and no cooling the room heated toward the ~150 F threshold at which heat-sensitive sprinkler plugs would spray and destroy the equipment. The author, living nearby, ran back, keyed into the room, and manually pulled power from every rack; the monitored temperature stopped at 143.6 F. Downtime was minimal because US markets were closed, and the post-incident review chose to keep the sprinklers and the in-office datacenter while tightening procedures. The detection had been pure luck (Hong Kong staff spotting many servers' rising temperatures), so the author wrote an OCaml monitor that polls each server's onboard temperature sensors every minute, averages them, and alerts on an elevated fleet-wide mean rather than trusting less reliable CRAC or room-sensor telemetry. The account is a self-reported, unverified first-person narrative, disclosed as human-written with AI editing.
novelty: insider war story on datacenter near-miss from fire-suppression design flaw
audience: infra/SRE engineers and datacenter operators interested in physical failure modes

title: Attention to Mamba: A Recipe for Cross-Architecture Distillation
why: If you want Mamba's throughput without training from scratch, this gives a distillation path that keeps a pretrained Transformer's quality on a pure SSM, no hybrid attention blocks left in the student.
notes: Two-stage recipe: distill the Transformer teacher into a linearized-attention model via an adaptation of the kernel trick, then distill that linearized model into an adapted Mamba that contains no attention blocks.
On Pythia-1B, the distilled Mamba reaches perplexity 14.01 against the teacher's 13.86; the authors claim downstream task performance largely carries over.

Framing claim: naive direct Transformer-to-Mamba distillation fails to preserve teacher performance, a limitation prior work patched with hybrid Attention+SSM blocks; the paper's argument is that principled Mamba initialization avoids the hybrid.

Evidence base: ablations at 1B scale with 10B tokens varying the sequence-mixer architecture, plus scaling analysis over model size and total distillation tokens, and a sensitivity analysis on how tokens are split between the two stages.
Stated caveat: gaps remain on downstream tasks that rely more on in-context recall, consistent with known SSM weaknesses versus attention.
From Apple Machine Learning Research; the perplexity and task numbers are self-reported by the authors, limited to the 1B / 10B-token regime shown.
summary: Apple researchers propose a two-stage method for distilling a pretrained Transformer into a pure Mamba state-space model that contains no attention blocks. The teacher is first distilled into a linearized version of attention using an adaptation of the kernel trick, then that linearized model is distilled into an adapted Mamba. The central claim is that a principled initialization of Mamba lets the student recover teacher quality without the hybrid attention/SSM blocks that prior cross-architecture distillation work relied on. On Pythia-1B, the distilled Mamba reaches perplexity 14.01 versus the teacher's 13.86, and the authors report that most downstream performance carries over, with gaps on tasks that depend on in-context recall. Claims are supported by ablations at 1B scale with 10B tokens, scaling analyses over model size and distillation tokens, and a sensitivity analysis on token allocation between the two stages. Numbers are self-reported and confined to the 1B regime described.
novelty: two-stage Transformer-to-Mamba distillation via linearized attention intermediate
audience: ML researchers/engineers building or converting SSM-based LLMs

title: No finite rulebook can certify every safe program: an impossibility theorem for gatekeeping AI agents
why: If you are building a gatekeeper that reads agent-written code and decides whether to run it, this paper proves the clean goal is unreachable: no finite, machine-checkable rulebook can both clear every safe program and block every unsafe one, so a static allow/deny policy will always either reject something safe or admit something it must refuse.
notes: The setup: an AI assistant writes small programs and a gatekeeper must decide from the code alone whether each may run, against fixed rules — never perform a forbidden action, never let output depend on a secret, always answer eventually.

Prohibitions are one-sided checkable: every violation can be caught by watching execution, but no safe program can be cleared for good, because 'never' is not settled by any finite record of behavior.
Confidentiality ('never leak a secret') and responsiveness ('always answer eventually') are neither confirmable nor refutable from finite evidence — both sides fail, not just one.

Quantitative bound claimed: any sound rulebook of n bits omits a compliant program of about n bits; adding a time limit makes everything checkable only by running the program for essentially the whole limit, so finite-checkable is not feasible-checkable.

Simulations on 2.2 million random programs plus self-referential adversaries indicate the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, and the one error a longer test never removes is the liveness part of confidentiality.
Proposed fallback: not a verdict on every program, but a checkable list guaranteed to contain everything the gatekeeper must allow and nothing it must refuse.
summary: The paper formalizes an AI-agent gatekeeping problem: a gatekeeper must decide, from code alone and backed by evidence a machine can check in finite time, whether a program obeys fixed safety rules (never do a forbidden action, never leak a secret, always answer eventually). It proves that an allow-list and a deny-list cannot both be complete under this constraint, because finite records settle neither 'never' nor 'eventually.' Prohibitions are one-sided: violations are catchable by watching, but no safe program is ever cleared permanently; confidentiality and responsiveness fail on both sides. The authors characterize exactly which rules about visible behavior evidence can confirm, show any sound n-bit rulebook omits a compliant program of about n bits, and argue a time limit restores checkability only at the cost of running nearly the full limit, so finite is not feasible. Simulations on 2.2 million random programs and self-referential adversaries suggest the obstruction is adversarial rather than typical, with the persistent residual error being the liveness part of confidentiality. The constructive takeaway is a fallback: a checkable list that includes everything the gatekeeper must allow and excludes everything it must refuse, instead of a universal verdict.
novelty: formal impossibility proof that no finite rulebook can fully gatekeep AI-agent code safety
audience: researchers/engineers building AI agent sandboxing, verification, or guardrail systems

title: Veritas: A Verifier Generation Harness for Agent Tasks
why: Self-improving agent loops stall on who grades each round; Veritas replaces hand-written verifiers with generated ones that, in the authors' tests, match official verdicts better than seven competing harnesses on every execution-scored benchmark.
notes: Veritas is a harness that auto-generates task verifiers, aimed at self-improving systems where a verifier judges each improvement round and hand-written verifiers do not scale to tasks shipped without one.

It adds three generation mechanisms on top of a general agent harness: an evidence header declaring what the verifier will observe, a library of domain rules that tasks leave unstated, and authoring principles partly refined by a self-improvement loop.
Evaluation spans six benchmarks (unnamed in the abstract): four scored by execution, whose official verifiers the authors first certify, and two that compare pairs of responses.

Self-reported results: with the model held fixed, Veritas verifiers agree better with official verdicts than seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks, and sit at or near best on the two pairwise benchmarks.
Also claimed to beat the vendor's own harness for two of three other model families, and to improve 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs when its mechanisms are added across three harnesses.
All figures are from the preprint; no external replication, methodology detail, or absolute agreement rates appear in the abstract, and benchmark identities are unspecified.
summary: Veritas is a harness that automatically generates verifiers for agent tasks, targeting self-improving systems whose quality depends on a verifier that judges each improvement round but that normally must be written by hand. Beyond a general-purpose agent harness, it adds an evidence header stating what the verifier will observe, a library of unstated domain rules, and authoring principles partly refined by a self-improvement loop. The authors evaluate on six benchmarks: four scored by execution (with official verifiers first certified) and two that compare pairs of responses. They report that, with the model fixed, Veritas verifiers agree with official verdicts better than seven other harnesses on all four execution-scored benchmarks and rank at or near best on the two pairwise ones, while also beating the vendor's own harness for two of three other model families. Its mechanisms are said to improve 9 of 12 harness-benchmark pairs across three harnesses. The claims are self-reported in a preprint; the abstract omits benchmark names, absolute scores, and replication.
novelty: automated verifier generation for self-improving agent systems
audience: researchers/engineers building self-improving agent/RL systems needing scalable reward verifiers

title: Open research, stronger privacy: Making Firefox users harder to fingerprint
why: If you ship a browser or build anti-fraud fingerprinting, Firefox just published a measured map of which signals actually distinguish 25M users and shipped defaults that shrink CPU core counts and screen metrics to collapse those signals.
notes: The study simulated the measurements collected by three commercial fingerprinting scripts: Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai, then analyzed how feature combinations distinguish users across nearly 25 million Firefox users.

Telemetry was collected over OHTTP: a relay saw the user IP but not request contents, while Mozilla saw contents without the IP; individual records were deleted months ago and only aggregates were retained for publication.

Concrete mitigations: screen resolution APIs no longer expose taskbar/dock size and position, and processor count is reported as 4 or 8 rather than the exact core count; additional fixes made image rendering, Web Audio, and math operations more consistent across users on Android.

Mozilla's self-reported evaluation claims the protections (most recent shipped in Firefox 145) reduced the number of users with unique fingerprints and enlarged shared-fingerprint groups; the article gives no magnitude numbers for the reduction.

Stated caveat: this does not make fingerprinting impossible since trackers can adapt, and separate randomization-based signals fall outside the reported measurements because their benefit is harder to quantify.

Rollout is staged: taskbar/dock hiding is on by default in all modes, while other protections land first in Private Browsing and Strict ETP before becoming default; the underlying paper is accepted at CCS 2026.
summary: Mozilla describes research, accepted at CCS 2026, measuring which browser and device signals most distinguish Firefox users and the mitigations it shipped in response. Using measurements from nearly 25 million Firefox users, collected over OHTTP so no party held both IP and request contents, the team simulated fingerprinting scripts from Fingerprint Pro, Signifyd, and Akamai to see which feature combinations single users out. It found that protecting a small number of features weakens popular techniques, and shipped changes including hiding taskbar/dock size via screen resolution APIs, reporting CPU core count as only 4 or 8, and making image rendering, Web Audio, and math operations more consistent on Android. Mozilla claims these protections, most recently in Firefox 145, reduced unique fingerprints and enlarged shared-fingerprint groups, though it reports no magnitude figures and notes trackers can adapt. Some protections are default in all modes; others ship first in Private Browsing and Strict ETP before wider default rollout. Individual telemetry was deleted and only aggregates retained; code, paper, and a test suite were published openly.
novelty: large-scale real-world fingerprinting measurement with shipped mitigations
audience: browser privacy/security engineers and researchers

title: The Surprising Effectiveness of Deleting Weights in LLM Post-Training
why: If the result holds, you can adapt a frontier-scale model by storing a binary mask hundreds to thousands of times smaller than a full checkpoint, with near-zero forgetting of prior tasks.
notes: Deletion Tuning learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks and makes no other change: it only zeros weights, fewer than 0.05% of them, and the paper claims this matches full fine-tuning (FFT) at scale.
Parity with FFT is claimed across three post-training regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR), supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation.
The trained mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than the corresponding FFT checkpoint, since it stores a sparse set of deleted-weight locations rather than updated weight values.
On continual learning, under RL the method's prior-task accuracy stays near the base model while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points.

Geometric analysis using stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap reports Deletion Tuning's weight changes are closest to FFT, closer than LoRA or random sparse fine-tuning; this is offered as the explanation for why masking alone suffices.
Abstract only: no model sizes, task benchmarks, baseline hyperparameters, or absolute accuracy numbers are given in the provided text, and all figures are author-reported.
summary: This arXiv paper introduces Deletion Tuning, a post-training method that acquires new capabilities by zeroing fewer than 0.05% of a pretrained LLM's weights and changing nothing else. It learns a binary mask over the gate projection of transformer blocks and claims to match full fine-tuning across three regimes: reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards, supervised fine-tuning, and on-policy distillation. Two claimed advantages are storage (the mask is hundreds to thousands of times smaller than an FFT checkpoint) and reduced forgetting: under RL the method keeps prior-task accuracy near the base level while FFT, LoRA, and random sparse fine-tuning lose up to 5.4 points. To explain why deletion alone works, the authors analyze the geometry of learned weight changes under RL via stable rank, spectrum drift, and principal-weight overlap, finding Deletion Tuning closest to FFT on all three measures. The provided text is the abstract only, so model scales, benchmarks, and absolute results are not specified, and the numbers are self-reported.
novelty: binary masking <0.05% of weights matches full fine-tuning
audience: ML researchers and engineers working on LLM post-training/continual learning

title: Sable: A Small-Field Sumcheck Argument for Bit-Exact Inference of Large Language Models
why: You can now get a cryptographic receipt that a specific open-weight 32B model produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, for about 6.4 cents of GPU time per 4,096-token request on a single card.
notes: Sable proves that a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced an exact token sequence, bit for bit. It fixes an integer function F_O with no floating-point step: every rounding, normalization, softmax, and sampling decision is determined by inputs, and the constraint relations provably never wrap modulo the 31-bit KoalaBear prime.

It batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits every witness tensor and weight in one multilinear commitment built from Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees, and a mixed-length BaseFold opening; the prover streams the model layer by layer on one GPU.

Reported timings on one NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell: all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5s for 4,096 tokens and 398s for 16,384 tokens; Qwen3-32B and MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B at 4,096 tokens in 121.8s and 84.7s. Proving costs 41-50x serving time, and 40-64x less time per parameter and token than zkLLM (self-reported).
Accuracy cost of the integer-only F_O: its greedy token matches the BF16 model at 86.3% of positions on WikiText-2, and on Qwen3 it lands within 1.6 points of BF16 on MMLU and 1.7 points on GSM8K.
Verification runs on one CPU core in 19-56s with a compiled core; round-by-round soundness error is 2^-103 in the random-oracle model.

The proof is not zero-knowledge, so it exposes weights and witnesses and is aimed only at open-weight models, not confidential ones. The 14% greedy-token divergence from BF16 is a caveat: Sable proves the integer model ran, not that it equals the floating-point reference.
summary: Sable is an argument system and single-GPU prover that certifies a committed, integer-quantized transformer produced a given token sequence from a given prompt, bit for bit. It replaces floating-point inference with a fully integer function F_O whose constraint relations provably never wrap the 31-bit KoalaBear prime, batches zerochecks and LogUp-GKR lookups into one sumcheck per domain, and commits all weights and witnesses in a single multilinear commitment (Reed-Solomon codes, BLAKE3 Merkle trees, mixed-length BaseFold). On one RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell GPU the authors report proving all 64 layers of Qwen2.5-32B in 92.5s for 4,096 tokens and 398s for 16,384 tokens, plus Qwen3-32B and the MoE Qwen3-30B-A3B, at roughly 6.4 cents per 4,096-token request and 40-64x less time per parameter and token than zkLLM (self-reported). The integer model trades some fidelity: its greedy token matches BF16 at 86.3% of WikiText-2 positions and stays within 1.6-1.7 points of BF16 on MMLU and GSM8K. A verifier checks a proof on one CPU core in 19-56s with round-by-round soundness error 2^-103 in the random-oracle model. Because the proof is not zero-knowledge, the system targets open-weight models only.
novelty: practical single-GPU ZK-proof of exact LLM inference, not just approximation
audience: cryptography/ML-systems researchers working on verifiable inference and model provenance

title: Atuin Threads: All your agent sessions on every machine
why: Your agent sessions, now scattered and lost across laptops and dev boxes, become a searchable, synced, end-to-end-encrypted record you can resume on any machine or hand to a different agent harness.
notes: Ships in Atuin 18.24+; `atuin resume` opens a TUI to search and resume sessions, and a session can be forked across machines or from one agent to another (start in Claude Code on a dev server, finish in Codex on a laptop).
Supported harnesses at launch: Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Omp, and OpenCode, with more promised. Session capture is opt-in.

Reuses Atuin's existing sync engine, which treats anything modelable as an append-only log; the author notes most AI sessions fit that shape. Synced data is end-to-end encrypted, so Atuin says it cannot read sessions; you can use hosted sync, self-host, or stay fully local.

An MCP server (`atuin mcp`, installable via `atuin mcp install claude/codex/pi/opencode`) lets agents themselves search and cite prior sessions, including abandoned work and the reasoning behind past decisions.
The pitch over shell history: agent sessions capture intent, command output, and discarded attempts in plain English, not just the commands that ran.
Team session-sharing (hand off a thread like a Git branch) is described as opt-in and in development, not shipped; the post solicits interested users.
summary: Atuin Threads, released in Atuin 18.24, extends the Atuin shell-history tool to capture, sync, and resume AI coding-agent sessions across machines and across different agents. Users run `atuin resume` to search past sessions in a TUI and can fork a session from one harness to another (e.g. Claude Code to Codex) or from one machine to another with context intact. It is built on Atuin's existing end-to-end encrypted sync engine for append-only logs, which the author says most agent sessions map onto; capture is opt-in, and sync can run on Atuin's hosted server, a self-hosted server, or stay local. Supported agents at launch are Claude Code, Codex, Pi, Omp, and OpenCode. An MCP server (`atuin mcp`) lets agents search and reference prior sessions directly, surfacing abandoned work and past reasoning. The author cites anecdotes (recovering unshipped onboarding work, tracing a Tigris object-store permissions failure, forking a benchmark investigation to a faster-disk Mac) and says an opt-in team session-sharing feature is still in development.
novelty: synced, resumable agent session history across machines/tools
audience: engineers using multiple AI coding agents across devices

title: EmbodiedLab: Benchmarking Embodied Agents That Act to Know
why: The strongest of six frontier coding agents solves fewer than half of these physical-discovery tasks under native control, and the failures cluster in manipulating the apparatus rather than in reasoning, a concrete gap for anyone building embodied or lab-automation agents.
notes: EmbodiedLab covers 30 experiments across five scientific disciplines on 14 apparatus platforms in a physics-based simulated lab; the agent is given an objective and the apparatus, picks its own procedure, and reads instruments through cameras.
System parameters are resampled for every instance, so outcomes cannot be known or memorized in advance, yet each task is scored exactly and every experiment is verified solvable.
Scoring checks both what the agent came to know (grounded in instrument readings recorded during the episode) and the physical state the task requires, separating knowing from acting.

Six frontier models were evaluated inside their developers' coding agents under three conditions: native observation/control, added perception and motion planning, and manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents.

With native control the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time; most failures across all agents come from interacting with the apparatus, and distilled manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception/planning do.

Positioned to fill a gap: manipulation benchmarks hand the agent a target state, while scientific-discovery benchmarks replace physical experimentation with symbolic actions or numeric queries. Self-reported by the authors; benchmark and evaluation code are released.
summary: EmbodiedLab is a benchmark for embodied agents that must "act to know": a robot changes the state of a simulated physics apparatus, observes feedback through cameras, and experiments until it discovers an unknown outcome, rather than driving toward a given target state. It spans 30 experiments in five disciplines across 14 apparatus platforms, resampling system parameters per instance so results cannot be known in advance but can be scored exactly, with every task verified solvable. Evaluation grades both what the agent learned (grounded in instrument readings logged during the episode) and the required physical state. The authors test six frontier models inside their developers' coding agents under three setups: native observation and control, added perception and motion planning, and manipulation skills distilled from the strongest agents. They report that under native control even the strongest agent succeeds less than half the time, that most failures stem from physically interacting with the apparatus rather than from reasoning, and that distilled manipulation skills help weaker agents more than perception and planning. The paper positions the benchmark between manipulation benchmarks (target state given) and scientific-discovery benchmarks (symbolic or numeric actions only), and releases the benchmark and evaluation code. Results are self-reported.
novelty: benchmark for agents that act to discover unknown physical outcomes, not just manipulate
audience: embodied AI / robotics researchers evaluating agent reasoning-via-interaction

title: A crypto and AI money guide to election night
why: If Sherrod Brown wins Ohio after crypto PACs dumped $64.2 million against him, the industry's implicit threat, "cross us and we end your career," stops being credible, which changes the calculus for every member of Congress weighing a crypto vote.
notes: Crypto super PACs spent $170.5M across 100 seats this cycle ($125.5M for Republicans, $45M for Democrats), already past the $130M they spent in 2024; AI PACs spent $79M across 68 seats leaning Democratic ($50.2M vs $28.8M). The median per-seat buy fell from $817K to $367K, with 26 seats drawing near-identical ~$150K buys.

Spending is concentrated, not broad: competitive races (Cook Toss-up/Lean) are 26% of contests but 72% of dollars; safe bets are 61% of contests but 18% of dollars. Ohio Senate, NY-12's Democratic primary, and Nebraska Senate alone account for $105.6M, nearly 60% of competitive spending.

Ohio's Senate special (Husted R vs. Brown D) is the single biggest tech-money race at $64.2M, almost all crypto. Fairshake's Defend American Jobs spent $36.9M for Husted and $19.7M against Brown; the spend began Sept 22, days after the Clarity Act failed cloture on Sept 15 with no Democratic votes and three Republican defections. Ads reportedly don't mention crypto. Brown led by 1.7-3.1 points in aggregators at the time of writing.

Crypto has stopped funding Democrats in general elections: in 2024 it spent ~$10M each to elect Slotkin and Gallego; this cycle its Democratic money is mostly primary attacks (e.g., $10M against Juliana Stratton in Illinois, who won by ~8 points) and ~$1M thank-you buys for safe incumbents who backed the Clarity and Genius Acts.

Two Fairshake-network PACs rank in the top ten super PACs by receipts; Leading the Future, the AI PAC backed by OpenAI president Greg Brockman and Andreessen Horowitz, ranks 13th. A new 'Building the Future' arm spent $2.5M on pro-data-center candidate Darline Graham in South Carolina.

Caveat: all figures are self-tracked by Molly White's one-person, reader-funded Tech Influence Watch, and candidate-specific donation totals come from the subset of crypto/AI companies and executives she tracks; crypto spending is a fraction of total race money (Ohio independent expenditures alone topped $350M).
summary: Molly White's Citation Needed election-night guide tallies $250M in combined crypto and AI super PAC spending on the 2026 federal midterms, via her Tech Influence Watch project. Crypto PACs spent $170.5M across 100 seats, tilting heavily Republican ($125.5M vs $45M), while AI PACs spent $79M across 68 seats favoring Democrats ($50.2M vs $28.8M). The money is concentrated: competitive races are 26% of contests but 72% of dollars, with Ohio's Senate special, NY-12's Democratic primary, and Nebraska's Senate race accounting for nearly 60% of competitive spending. Ohio is the marquee fight, where Fairshake's network poured $56.6M (part of $64.2M total) against longtime crypto critic Sherrod Brown after the Clarity Act died in the Senate in September; a Brown win would, per the piece and a quoted GOP crypto lobbyist, undermine the industry's reputation for punishing opponents. White also documents crypto abandoning the Democratic general-election support it gave Slotkin and Gallego in 2024, PACs mostly backing safe winners to pad win rates, and AI-sector fights centered on data-center siting. All figures are self-reported from a one-person, reader-funded operation covering a tracked subset of companies and executives.
novelty: crypto/AI PAC spending concentrated in few races, shifting toward GOP
audience: policy-watchers and engineers tracking tech industry political influence

title: One namespace to namespace them all (Python Language Summit 2026)
why: The flat import namespace that makes a stray math.py break random.randint is now on the table for a fix, and the same change could let Python ship stdlib modules on PyPI versioned apart from the interpreter.
notes: Pablo Galindo Salgado (Steering Council, Release Manager) proposed a top-level 'std' namespace so 'import std.json' or 'from std import json' guarantees the stdlib module; 'import json' would keep working indefinitely, and 'std.json is json' stays True.

Root cause framed as Python's flat namespace: a local json.py or math.py on sys.path (cwd or PYTHONPATH) shadows the stdlib, surfacing as later AttributeErrors. The -P flag (since 3.11) stops prepending unsafe paths but is rarely used.
The namespace also forces awkward stdlib names to dodge PyPI collisions: tomllib, graphlib, zoneinfo instead of toml, graph, timezone; adopting PyYAML's 'yaml' module hits the same constraint.

Pablo floated introducing new modules only under std (so plain 'import new_stdlib_module' would ImportError) to push adoption. Guido confirmed every stdlib module would eventually migrate, described as 'mostly mechanical,' possibly freezing all modules; Peter Bierma asked about perf cost, Pablo said 'effectively zero.'

Claimed side benefit: 'unbundling' the stdlib to ship modules via PyPI with independent versioning and out-of-band security fixes. Cautionary case cited is Ruby's gemified stdlib: 3-cycle deprecation for require, transitive-dependency warnings, and an unpatched uri-gem CVE because it wasn't in the Gemfile.

Stefan Behnel's 'from std import random' variant (keeping module names unchanged, avoiding sys.modules duplication) drew support; Guido suggested 'from std' could be magic, Pablo a 'special keyword,' with David Hewitt citing the new 3.15 'lazy' keyword as precedent. A show of hands found no one hated it. Gregory P. Smith warned the proposal bundles multiple problems and urged scoping. Jukka Lehtosalo noted there is no data on how often shadowing occurs.
summary: At the Python Language Summit 2026, Pablo Galindo Salgado proposed adding a top-level 'std' namespace so developers can write 'import std.json' or 'from std import json' to guarantee they get the standard library rather than a shadowing local file; plain 'import json' would keep working and resolve to the same object. He argued the deeper problem of Python's flat namespace is that it forces core developers into awkward stdlib names (tomllib, graphlib, zoneinfo) to avoid PyPI collisions, not just the beginner-facing AttributeError from a stray math.py. A potential side effect is 'unbundling' the stdlib to distribute modules via PyPI with independent versioning and out-of-band security fixes, with Ruby's gemified stdlib cited as a cautionary tale (long deprecations, an unpatched uri CVE). Migration would touch every stdlib module but was described as mostly mechanical with effectively zero runtime cost. Attendees reacted positively to a keyword-based 'from std' variant that leaves module names unchanged, while Gregory P. Smith cautioned the proposal conflates several problems and should be scoped narrowly. No concrete data exists on how often shadowing actually bites users.
novelty: proposal for std namespace to fix flat module shadowing in Python
audience: Python core devs and engineers debugging stdlib shadowing bugs

title: Garbage Collection: Generational? Incremental? Both! (Python Language Summit 2026)
why: If you fine-tuned CPython's GC generations in production to dodge multi-second pauses, that tuning is a moving target: 3.14 shipped an incremental GC, reverted it, and the next default is now up for debate.
notes: Python 3.14 shipped Mark Shannon's incremental, non-generational GC (single generation covering the whole heap) to cut peak pause times by ~an order of magnitude, then reverted to 3.13's generational GC after reports of significant memory pressure in production.

Claimed pause numbers: incremental GC cut peak pauses to tens of milliseconds versus around 3 seconds for the generational GC, at the cost of higher memory use. Self-reported, no methodology given in the talk writeup.

GC is a backup, not the primary collector: reference counting does the main work, and GC only finds unreachable cycles. GC is cited at ~11.67% of execution time vs 30.6% for the interpreter; a JIT would speed the interpreter but not memory management.

Scavenge effectiveness (objects collected / objects visited) is called 'pretty poor': 0.3% for the generational GC, ~1% for the reverted incremental GC. Shannon says comparing to other languages' GCs is unfair since 'nobody else does reference-counting and garbage collection.'
Proposed hybrid: two generations (young fixed initially at 20MB, plus old), alternating young/old incremental scavengers, old generation scavenged at twice the young survivor rate.

Tuning dispute: Shannon opposes JVM-style GC knobs because GC is only a backup in Python; Pablo Galindo and Thomas Wouters report live-tuning GC generations in production to remediate pathological behavior and to unblock version upgrades, and Shannon asked for those numbers before deciding. Larry Hastings' lock-free concurrent GC idea was called impractical because C extensions 'can do whatever they want.'
summary: At the Python Language Summit 2026, Mark Shannon presented work on CPython's garbage collector following the Python 3.14 reversion of his incremental GC back to 3.13's generational GC after reports of significant memory pressure in production. He framed GC as a backup to reference counting, responsible only for unreachable cycles, consuming roughly 11.67% of execution time, and introduced 'scavenge effectiveness' (objects collected / objects visited), measured at 0.3% for the generational GC and ~1% for the incremental one. The incremental GC reportedly cut peak pauses from ~3 seconds to tens of milliseconds but increased memory usage because it was non-generational. Shannon proposed a hybrid: two generations (young fixed initially at 20MB, old), alternating incremental scavengers, with the old generation scavenged at twice the young survivor rate. Core developers debated exposing JVM-style tuning knobs; Shannon resisted, while Pablo Galindo and Thomas Wouters argued live GC tuning is needed to fix pathological behavior and unblock Python upgrades, and Shannon asked for those numbers before deciding. A lock-free concurrent GC was dismissed as impractical given that C extensions can manipulate memory arbitrarily.
novelty: proposed hybrid two-generation incremental scavenger design for CPython GC
audience: CPython core devs and engineers tuning Python memory/latency in production

title: Memory Snapshots for CPython (Python Language Summit 2026)
why: If this lands, a Python interpreter in WebAssembly/edge runtimes starts roughly 4x faster by restoring a post-init memory image instead of re-running initialization, but it requires a new language-level re-init phase to avoid freezing the hash seed.
notes: In a Pyodide test, loading the interpreter from a memory snapshot ran 'Hello, world' in 0.353s versus 1.406s from scratch, about 4x faster (single reported case, no methodology given).

The core conflict: Python 3.3 added a randomized per-process salt to hash() to stop hash-collision DoS attacks against dict/set; a restored snapshot would freeze that seed to a fixed value shared across every restore, re-opening the attack.
Node.js shipped V8 snapshots in v4.2.4 for ~33% faster startup, then disabled them in v4.8.4 over the same class of determinism/security problem.

Hood Chatham proposes adding an explicit 'initialization phase' to the language model, citing RPython and SPy, so the runtime and third-party libraries can re-run and reintroduce randomness after a restore; Stefan Behnel suggested an atexit-style reinit callback.

PEP 810 lazy imports (Python 3.15) cut against this: snapshots win by paying parse/execute import cost once and restoring it, but lazy, unresolved imports never enter the snapshot, so their cost is paid every run; lazy imports also assume a runtime filesystem that edge compute often lacks.

Prior art cited: Alibaba's memory-dump-plus-metadata-table approach, and the Faster CPython team's finding that deep-freezing modules barely helped startup while adding complexity (cause not investigated); Eric Snow mentioned a copy-on-write freezing alternative.
summary: At the 2026 Python Language Summit, Hood Chatham proposed letting CPython boot from a memory snapshot taken after initialization instead of re-running init each time, targeting WebAssembly and edge-compute use cases where no runtime filesystem exists. A Pyodide test showed about 4x faster startup (0.353s vs 1.406s for 'Hello, world'), and Node.js saw ~33% gains with V8 snapshots before disabling them over a related issue. The central obstacle is hash-seed randomization, added in Python 3.3 to prevent hash-collision DoS: a restored snapshot would reuse one fixed seed across all processes, and other libraries likely make similar fresh-randomness assumptions. Chatham proposes adding an explicit 'initialization phase' to the language model (citing RPython and SPy) that can re-run on restore to reintroduce randomness. Discussion covered an atexit-style reinit callback, whether faster init or PEP 810 lazy imports (Python 3.15) could substitute, and prior art including Alibaba's memory-dump approach and the Faster CPython team's finding that deep-freezing modules didn't meaningfully improve startup. Chatham argued speeding up the interpreter is 'an order of magnitude more complex' than snapshotting, and that lazy imports would make his case worse because unresolved imports never enter the snapshot.
novelty: CPython memory-snapshot startup proposal and its hash-seed security conflict
audience: Python core devs and engineers optimizing interpreter startup (e.g. serverless/WASM)

title: Free-Threaded Python Post-Era (Python Language Summit 2026)
why: Now that PEP 779 put free-threaded Python on a supported track, the stdlib concurrency API is up for grabs, and this talk is the first concrete proposal for what sits above raw threads: a deadlock-free task model you can already pip install as bocpy.
notes: Behavior-Oriented Concurrency (BOC) is task-based: tasks are lightweight, run on any core, and are claimed to be unable to deadlock. Data is wrapped in data-aware mutexes called 'Cowns' (concurrent owners), and the @when(cown, ...) decorator declares which Cowns a task needs. The scheduler builds a dependency graph across tasks and data and, the presenters claim, can detect deadlocks or data races ahead of execution and raise them as exceptions.

The proof of concept, bocpy, is on PyPI (pip install bocpy) and runs on stable Python via subinterpreters. Because it uses stable Python, only isolation is implemented; the presenters say ownership and PEP 795 immutability cannot be done as a third-party library and require runtime changes. Performance is self-described as 'good for programs that aren't communication dominated,' since subinterpreter communication is expensive.

Framing device: a fast/simple/safe triangle. C is fast+simple but unsafe; Erlang is safe+simple but slow (copies data between actors); Rust is fast+safe but not simple (fighting the borrow checker). GIL Python is simple but not fully safe ('only protects the runtime'); subinterpreters are safe but neither simple nor fast; free-threaded Python is simple+fast but pushes correctness onto the programmer. The trio argued a high-level model should prioritize safety, then performance, then simplicity.

Presented at Python Language Summit 2026 by Tobias Wrigstad, Fridtjof Stoldt, and Donghee Na, following up their 2025 'Fearless Concurrency' talk. It addresses the one unmet PEP 779 acceptance criterion: the Steering Council asked the core team to propose higher-level concurrency primitives, suggesting the stdlib concurrent package where appropriate.

Pushback in discussion: Thomas Wouters cited past failures building universal subprocess/multiprocessing/threading interfaces (corner cases, suboptimal performance) and asked why bocpy would differ. Larry Hastings welcomed the research but opposed 'anointing a single way.' David Hewitt and Fridtjof pointed to Rust's async as a cautionary tale where the lack of a standard runtime interface 'forced' the ecosystem onto Tokio; Hewitt said an abstraction would be hard but still worth attempting.

Cited prior art for inspiration: Rust's ownership/borrowing, Go's channels and goroutines, Erlang's actors and message passing. Two further proofs of concept that modify the CPython runtime are in progress: one organizing the heap into isolated object groups so ownership violations raise from Cowns, and one implementing object immutability (PEP 795).
summary: At the Python Language Summit 2026, Tobias Wrigstad, Fridtjof Stoldt, and Donghee Na proposed Behavior-Oriented Concurrency (BOC) as a high-level concurrency interface for free-threaded Python, addressing the unmet PEP 779 criterion that the core team propose primitives safer than raw threads. BOC is task-based: data lives in data-aware mutexes called 'Cowns,' and tasks declare their dependencies via a @when decorator, letting a scheduler build a task/data dependency graph that the presenters claim guarantees no deadlocks and no data races, converting such conflicts into exceptions before execution. The design is framed against a fast/simple/safe triangle (C, Erlang, Rust, plus Python's GIL, subinterpreters, and free-threading), with the trio arguing safety should rank above performance and simplicity. A proof of concept, bocpy, is published on PyPI and built on subinterpreters running stable Python, so only isolation (not ownership or PEP 795 immutability, which need runtime changes) is implemented, and performance degrades for communication-heavy programs. Discussion was skeptical: Thomas Wouters doubted a universal interface would avoid the corner cases that plagued prior stdlib attempts, and Larry Hastings opposed blessing any single model, while both sides cited Rust's fragmented async ecosystem as a reason the stdlib should still try to provide an abstraction. Two additional runtime-modifying proofs of concept, for heap isolation and object immutability, are in progress.
novelty: BOC proposal: deadlock-free task/mutex concurrency model for Python
audience: Python core devs and engineers tracking free-threading/concurrency changes

title: Lightning Talks (Python Language Summit 2026)
why: CPython's core team signaled no objection to an AGENTS.md for agent-driven PRs and sees agent contribution volume as a real threat to the open-contribution model, while the fix for a faster GC is now blocked on free-threading becoming the sole Stable ABI.
notes: Mark Shannon wants the 32 spare high bits in PyObject's ob_refcnt header (treated as a 32-bit int since PEP 683 in Python 3.12) for a better GC and faster allocations; using them breaks the Stable ABI. Thomas Wouters' resolution: wait until free-threading's abi3t becomes the only Stable ABI, since free-threaded Python never promised object-layout compatibility. No appetite to break the existing Stable ABI now.

Daniele Parmeggiani proposed 'uninterruptible scopes': context managers whose __enter__/__exit__ are shielded from interruption so cleanup is guaranteed. The underlying interrupt/cancellation machinery already exists in CPython but is unexposed at the Python level because it is a 'huge source of footguns'; the signal module docs currently advise turning signals off. Cost: more bytecode.

Gregory P. Smith and Lukasz Langa floated adding a simple AGENTS.md (linking to the Developer Guide) to curb low-quality LLM-agent PRs; a show-of-hands found no core dev opposed. Greg said the file would stay simple, 'seldom change,' and PRs modifying it would be rejected.

Seth Larson reported the Python Security Response Team saw increased LLM-generated vulnerability reports; policy changes plus a new threat model appeared to help, though the effect was hard to prove. Lukasz Langa voiced pessimism that CPython may eventually have to stop accepting many outside contributions due to agent-driven volume.
Ken Jin asked core devs to read PEP 836 (JIT) and say what they disagree with, noting only 33 replies on the discussion thread so far.
Kushal Das presented EktuPy, a project bringing Scratch-style block-based and 'remix' concepts to teach Python to programmers who started on Scratch.
summary: Reporting from the Python Language Summit 2026 lightning talks, this post covers six short CPython-internals pitches. Mark Shannon wants to repurpose 32 spare bits in PyObject's ob_refcnt header (a 32-bit int since PEP 683) for a faster GC and allocator, which would break the Stable ABI; the agreed path is to wait until free-threading's abi3t becomes the sole Stable ABI, since it never promised object-layout stability. Daniele Parmeggiani proposed 'uninterruptible scopes' to safely shield context-manager cleanup from cancellation in structured concurrency, exposing interrupt machinery that already exists in CPython but is hidden because it is footgun-prone. Gregory P. Smith and Lukasz Langa proposed a minimal, rarely-changed AGENTS.md to improve LLM-agent PR quality, with no core-dev objection in a show of hands; related discussion noted rising LLM-generated security reports and Langa's worry that CPython may eventually have to limit outside contributions. Ken Jin asked for more feedback on PEP 836 (JIT), having received only 33 replies, and Kushal Das showed EktuPy, a Scratch-inspired on-ramp to Python.
novelty: CPython internals debates: ABI header bits, interrupt safety, AGENTS.md adoption
audience: Python core devs and CPython internals-curious engineers

title: Modality-Aware Expert Pruning for MoE-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
why: A training-free pass drops a ~58GB MoE-MLLM (InternVL3.5-30B-A3B, Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B) onto one 40GB GPU by cutting ~27GB of expert weights, no fine-tuning required.
notes: Expert parameters dominate MoE-MLLM memory: >90% of model size, e.g. 54GB of ~58GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B, despite only a few experts activating per token.

MAEP splits expert importance by modality in a single forward pass, treating text-side importance as a preservation signal and vision-side importance as the pruning signal; experts are ranked globally across layers rather than per-layer.

Two mechanisms: Delta-H Output, which measures the change in MoE output when an expert is removed (redistribution-aware), and low-attention vision tokens as a vision-side signal the authors report keeps a stable expert-importance ranking across datasets.
Claimed result: ~27GB reduction in BF16 expert weight footprint, about 47% of total memory, enough to fit a ~58GB model into a single 40GB GPU.

Evaluated on three MoE-based MLLMs across multimodal and text benchmarks; authors report it beats modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks while staying competitive on text-only tasks. Code is linked.
Caveats: benchmark names, baseline identities, prune ratios, and accuracy deltas are not given in the abstract; the dataset-stability of the vision signal is asserted, not quantified here.
summary: MAEP (Modality-Aware Expert Pruning) is a training-free method for compressing Mixture-of-Experts multimodal LLMs, where expert parameters account for over 90% of model size (e.g. 54GB of ~58GB in BF16 for InternVL3.5-30B-A3B and Qwen3-VL-30B-A3B). Unlike prior pruning that aggregates expert importance uniformly across tokens, MAEP decomposes importance by modality in a single forward pass: text-side importance acts as a preservation signal and vision-side importance as the pruning signal, with experts ranked globally across layers. It relies on a Delta-H Output metric (the MoE output change when an expert is removed) and on low-attention vision tokens, which the authors report give a dataset-stable importance ranking. On three MoE-based MLLMs the authors claim MAEP beats modality-agnostic baselines on most multimodal benchmarks while staying competitive on text-only tasks, cutting the BF16 expert footprint by ~27GB (~47% of total memory) so a ~58GB model fits on a single 40GB GPU. The abstract omits specific benchmarks, baselines, prune ratios, and accuracy numbers; code is released.
novelty: training-free modality-split expert pruning cuts MoE-MLLM memory 47%
audience: ML engineers deploying large MoE multimodal models under GPU memory constraints

title: What's new in the .NET 11 runtime
why: If you ship .NET apps, .NET 11 will refuse to start on pre-2013 x86/x64 CPUs (baseline jumps to x86-64-v2) and introduces a preview async model that moves state machines out of the compiler and into the runtime, changing what your stack traces and allocations look like.
notes: x86/x64 JIT/AOT minimum rises from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 on all OSes, now guaranteeing CX16, POPCNT, SSE3, SSSE3, SSE4.1, SSE4.2; ReadyToRun targets x86-64-v3 (adds AVX, AVX2, BMI1/2, F16C, FMA, LZCNT, MOVBE) on Windows/Linux but not Apple. Older CPUs fail to launch with a 'current CPU is missing one or more of the baseline instruction sets' message.

Arm64: Windows minimum now requires LSE and R2R target moves to armv8.2-a + RCPC; Linux R2R adds LSE (possible extra jitting overhead at launch); Apple M1 baseline unchanged. Microsoft frames the cut as reducing codebase maintenance complexity and matching OS-enforced hardware requirements.

Runtime Async V2 (preview, opt in via <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>) has the runtime, not the compiler, manage async suspension/resumption; the .NET runtime libraries themselves are now compiled with it and contain no compiler-generated state machines. Opt out per project with <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync>; the DOTNET_RuntimeAsync and UNSUPPORTED_RuntimeAsync env vars are removed. The product team asks for throughput and library-size reports rather than citing its own numbers.

Live stack traces shrink from 13 frames to 5 in the article's three-deep async example because state-machine infrastructure frames disappear; exception stack traces are unchanged. Runtime Async supports NativeAOT and R2R, reuses continuation objects, and skips saving unchanged locals.

Claimed, self-reported speedups: up to 20x for collection ops using Comparer<T>.Default/EqualityComparer<T>.Default now specialized in R2R images; up to 200x for interface-heavy code on non-JIT platforms like iOS via cached interface dispatch; ~12% faster Guid.NewGuid() on Linux using getrandom() with batch caching instead of /dev/urandom; 5-50% on Arm64 IndexOfAnyAsciiSearcher workloads. None include benchmark methodology.

Written against release candidate 2. Other changes: async continuations can skip ExecutionContext capture/restore when there is nothing to restore; runtime now initializes on machines with more than 1024 logical processors (GC keeps its 1024-heap limit); in-process crash reporting via DOTNET_EnableCrashReport=1; JIT bounds-check and devirtualization improvements; new SVE2/AVX-VNNI-512 intrinsics and SIMD lane construction APIs.
summary: Microsoft's .NET 11 runtime notes (written for RC2) cover two load-bearing changes. First, minimum hardware baselines rise: x86/x64 moves from x86-64-v1 to x86-64-v2 across Apple, Linux, and Windows, with ReadyToRun compiling for x86-64-v3 on Windows and Linux; Arm64 Windows now requires LSE and targets armv8.2-a + RCPC. Apps on unsupported older CPUs fail to start with an explicit missing-instruction-set error. Microsoft justifies the cut as reducing codebase complexity and aligning with OS-enforced requirements. Second, Runtime Async V2 (preview, opt in via <Features>runtime-async=on</Features>) relocates async suspension and resumption from compiler-generated state machines into the runtime, producing shorter live stack traces (13 frames down to 5 in the example), lower allocation pressure, and support for NativeAOT and R2R; the runtime libraries themselves are already compiled with it, and the old DOTNET_RuntimeAsync env vars are replaced by a <UseRuntimeAsync>false</UseRuntimeAsync> opt-out. The document also lists many JIT, VM, WebAssembly, and NativeAOT optimizations with vendor-reported speedups (up to 20x for default-comparer collection ops in R2R, up to 200x for interface dispatch on non-JIT platforms, ~12% for Linux Guid.NewGuid), none accompanied by benchmark methodology.
novelty: runtime-native async replaces compiler state machines, raises CPU baseline
audience: .NET engineers and platform/infra teams planning upgrades

title: The Hardest Tarball?
why: One crafted pax tarball makes 20-plus mainstream tar implementations disagree, so any system that unpacks untrusted archives has a parser-differential attack surface you can test against today.
notes: The archive is built with a single GNU tar call: pax format, delete the ?time and size fields, rename a hard link to 'café' (forcing a UTF-8 pax header), then set size=512 on that hard link whose default size is 0. 512 is exactly one tar header block, so the ambiguous bytes are the header of the following empty file.

Eight distinct extraction outcomes result. GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go, and Perl ignore the size and extract file, café, and empty correctly. bsdtar (macOS system tar) writes the 512 bytes into the hard link, so file ends up containing empty's tar header.

7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, Rust's tar, and astral-tokio-tar treat the 512 bytes as hard-link data but skip them, dropping empty. Java Commons Compress writes empty's header into a separate file; PHP PharData makes café an empty file and still extracts empty; RubyGems drops café and creates a stray PaxHeaders directory; R applies the size to empty, filling it with 512 null bytes from the end-of-archive marker.

Haskell's tar matches GNU behavior but has a string-decoding bug that writes 'cafÃ©' to disk. .NET, Julia, and uv's tar-codec reject the archive outright; the author argues rejection is the safest response even though it is not strictly POSIX-compliant.
The root ambiguity: POSIX says data blocks for a hard link 'may be included' in pax archives, leaving undefined whether a hard link can carry size and contents distinct from its original.
This is one of 134 cases in the author's haampie/tar-minefield test suite; results across implementations are tabulated at stoppels.ch/tar.
summary: A crafted tarball, buildable with a single GNU tar invocation, extracts eight different ways across well-known tar tools because it puts a pax size=512 record (one header block) on a hard-link entry whose size should be 0, exploiting undefined POSIX behavior about whether a hard link's data blocks 'may be included.' GNU tar, BusyBox, Python, Go, and Perl ignore the size and extract correctly; bsdtar writes the bytes into the hard link, corrupting its contents; 7-Zip, node-tar, tar-fs, and Rust's tar skip the data and drop the empty file; Java Commons Compress, PHP PharData, RubyGems, and R each produce their own divergent or corrupted output; Haskell's tar additionally mangles the UTF-8 filename. .NET, Julia, and uv's tar-codec reject the archive, which the author considers the safest behavior despite not being strictly POSIX-compliant. The tarball is one of 134 cases in the author's haampie/tar-minefield test suite, with a per-implementation comparison table published at stoppels.ch/tar.
novelty: crafted pax tarball extracts 8 different ways across tools
audience: systems/devtools engineers dealing with archive format edge cases and security implications
